text: AlterEcho: An Auditable Earth–Planetary Terrain Analogue System
Overall project paper · Team AlterEcho · NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 · 15 November 2026

AlterEcho is a research-shortlisting application that compares registered 10 km Earth windows with specific Mars or lunar reference windows. It combines traceable elevation data, deterministic terrain measurements, explicit quality gates and a bounded similarity index. The system is designed to make every number inspectable: the interface, API, exported JSON and this paper use the same versioned calculation inputs.
Abstract

Earth analogues are useful only when the question, scale, measurement and uncertainty are explicit. AlterEcho implements one narrow, reproducible question: whether the distributions of slope and relative elevation in a 10 km Earth window resemble those in a 10 km planetary reference at a 60 m grid. It measures four terrain descriptors, scores only two nonredundant distributions, calibrates tolerances from unselected Earth terrain, and reports a scenario range and background share beside the index. A candidate is not ranked when critical evidence is missing or when the tested resolution cannot separate it from the reference. The current atlas contains seven measured Earth candidates, five Mars references and one lunar distance-only reference. In the worked Atacama-south/Jezero comparison, the index is 97.90, but 17% of the 88 background windows score at least as high and both feature differences are within the tested resolution floor. The result therefore supports a limited low-relief terrain analogy, not a claim about geology, habitability, resources, landing safety or mission suitability.

text: How to read this paper

Sections 1–4 explain the product, data and software path. Sections 5–8 define the terrain measurements, formulas, tolerances, eligibility and ranking. Sections 9–11 show a worked result, discrimination checks and limitations. A source link means the official landing page or API used to identify a product; a local checksum means the exact byte file used by the current release. Planned or contextual products are listed for traceability but are never silently treated as scored evidence.
System architecture and user workflow

The browser is a Next.js application. It requests catalog, methodology, comparison, imagery, terrain-preview, provenance and report data from a FastAPI service. Python owns raster preparation and all scientific arithmetic; the frontend formats responses and never recomputes the index. Committed small artifacts make the atlas browseable without a provider call. Separate acquisition scripts are used only when a raw product must be restored or a new study window is deliberately registered.
architecture

A typical user selects a planetary body and reference, chooses a task profile, selects an Earth candidate, reads the simple result, opens full evidence, compares the two windows at a common scale, and exports the JSON record. The Explore page can screen a new Earth coordinate, but Explore output is a screening record and is not added to the ranked atlas. The Report page is a printable view of the same stored comparison.

text: The local release records 14 terrain inputs and 13 imagery records. Verified terrain bytes include eight Earth SRTM inputs, five Mars DEM inputs and one lunar derivative. The original Atacama window remains catalogued but excluded because it contains an industrial complex; Atacama south is the registered replacement. Raw files are ignored by Git, while manifests, derived artifacts and LF-normalized metadata hashes are retained.
Acquisition, processing and provenance

The reproducible path is: discover an official product; record its product, licence, AOI, asset and quality metadata; acquire only into ignored raw storage; verify size, host, checksum and raster metadata; process a 10 km core with a 1200 m halo; apply the documented quality mask; compute terrain features and quantiles; write a versioned artifact and manifest; and validate the artifact before serving it. A changed archive cannot overwrite a recorded raw checksum. Unsafe archive paths and replacement of differing raw bytes are rejected.

Each result carries an identity made from the Earth window, planetary reference, task, epoch, method version and profile configuration. It also exposes hashes for the method configuration, calibration, background population and selected calculation inputs. These controls answer “which bytes and rules made this number?” They do not claim that the source measurements or scientific interpretation have been independently validated.

text: Release verification and reproducibility

A release is considered internally reproducible when the catalog integrity audit, source-manifest audit, independent result recomputation, paper-number test and frontend build all pass. Backend tests cover the pure arithmetic, quantile approximation, eligibility gates, provenance and security boundaries. The frontend contract tests confirm that the displayed candidate, tie label, evidence panel and downloaded JSON correspond to the API response. These are engineering and numerical-consistency checks, not a substitute for external scientific validation.

text: Interpretation rules for users

items: Read the reference AOI, method version, grid and evidence coverage before comparing two indices. Results from different keys are not a competition.
Treat a high index as similarity of the measured distributions at the stated scale. Inspect the background share and scenario range before calling a candidate distinctive.
Treat a tie as an honest unresolved ordering, not a frontend error. A label such as “1 (tie)” means the candidate belongs to a range-overlap group.
Treat “not resolved” as a measurement statement: the observed distance is no larger than the tested placement and DEM-product floor. It is not proof that the surfaces are identical.
Do not interpret evidence coverage as confidence. A profile can have a high terrain score while remaining incomplete for geology, temperature, water, habitability or field testing.

text: Validation roadmap

The next scientific step is not to tune the index until the ranking looks persuasive. It is to pre-register expert-labelled positive analogues, deliberately selected negative controls and held-out regions, then evaluate calibration, discrimination and stability without changing the tolerances after seeing the labels. Additional families should be admitted only when Earth and planetary observations have comparable support, resolution, epoch and uncertainty. Morphology descriptors that preserve spatial arrangement, explicit vertical-datum checks, surface-process evidence and field-observation protocols are promising extensions. Until those tests are complete, AlterEcho should be used as an auditable terrain-screening aid and a way to expose assumptions—not as a site-certification system.
Methods: Earth–Planetary Terrain Analogue Comparison

This section describes the method implemented in the AlterEcho application as analogue-method-v1.0 with the terrain measurement terrain-v5.0. Every number below is generated from the versioned configuration, calibration files and a live comparison of the running backend; a test fails if the text and the backend diverge.
Research question and scope

We ask a narrow question: at a specified 10 km Earth window and a specified 10 km planetary reference window, how closely do the distributions of two measured terrain properties agree on a common 60 m grid, and is that agreement larger than what the measurement itself can resolve? A result is conditional on the comparison definition

where $E$ is the Earth area of interest (AOI), $P$ the planetary reference AOI, $T$ the task profile, $H$ the epoch (the present-day surface recorded by the elevation models, not the ancient environment that formed it) $V$ the method version and $R$ the profile configuration (identified by its content digest). Results with different definitions are never ranked together. The output is an experimental terrain evidence index, not a probability that a place is like Mars, not a measure of geology, atmosphere, water, habitability, access or mission safety, and not a NASA or USGS endorsement.
Areas of interest and sources

Earth windows are 10 km squares centred on registered points and processed from NASA SRTMGL1.003 (1 arc-second, about 30 m; elevations in metres above the EGM96 geoid; acquired February 2000). The Jezero reference (mars-jezero-aoi-v1, centred at 18.44° N, 77.45° E) uses the Mars 2020 Science Investigation CTX DEM mosaic (20 m posting; DOI 10.5066/P906QQT8). Four further Mars references (Gale crater floor, Elysium Planitia at the InSight site, Gusev crater plains and the Eberswalde delta) use USGS controlled CTX DTMs (20 m; CC0; DOI 10.5066/P9JKVWR3), read as windows from cloud-optimised GeoTIFFs and reprojected once onto a local equirectangular grid true to scale at the window latitude. Among products covering a window, the one with the lowest median stereo intersection error was used. A lunar south-pole window uses LRO LOLA LDEM_875S_20M. Windows were placed by documented rules before their terrain was measured; one Earth window (the original Atacama window) was excluded because it contains an industrial complex and was replaced by a window 8 km south.
Raster preparation and quality rules

Each DEM is resampled bilinearly from its native posting onto a north-up metric grid centred on the AOI: UTM for Earth, the native or local equirectangular grid for Mars and polar stereographic for the Moon. All three are true to scale over a 10 km window to better than 0.1 %. The primary analysis grid is 60 m (167 × 167 cells, at least twice the native posting); 120 and 240 m grids are used only as sensitivity scenarios. A 1200 m halo is processed around every window so neighbourhood statistics are complete at the edges, and only core cells are summarised. Source no-data become missing values and are never filled. On Earth, cells that are at least half built-up in ESA WorldCover v200 (2021) are set to missing before derivatives are computed. A feature is eligible only if at least 90% of core cells are valid on both windows.

Four terrain constructs are measured on every valid cell: slope; local relief (maximum minus minimum elevation in a 17 × 17-cell, 1020 m neighbourhood); roughness (standard deviation of elevation in a 5 × 5-cell, 300 m neighbourhood); and relative elevation. Neighbourhood statistics require at least half the window to be valid. Slope uses central differences on the metric grid,

For a scalar feature $k$ measured in the same units on both bodies, the difference is

No scalar feature is scored in the current version; all scored terrain features are distributions. For a distribution feature, $F_{E,k}$ and $F_{P,k}$ are the empirical cumulative distribution functions of the valid core cells (equal-area cells, so every cell has the same weight), and the distance is the one-dimensional Wasserstein-1 distance
in degrees for slope and metres for relative elevation. The implementation evaluates Equation 5 with the midpoint rule on 500 quantiles,

where $Q$ is the inverted-CDF empirical quantile function. For the worked example below, the quantile approximation differs from the exact all-cell W1 by 0.0005 ° (0.06 %) for slope; 0.0093 m (0.06 %) for relative elevation. W1 compares distributions only: two windows with the same slope histogram but different arrangements of ridges, channels or craters have zero distance.
Feature similarity and tolerances
Each distance is converted to a bounded feature similarity

so that $s_k = 1$ at $d_k = 0$, $s_k = 0.5$ at $d_k = \tau_k$ and $s_k = 0.0625$ at $d_k = 2\tau_k$ (these values are unit-tested). The tolerance $\tau_k$ has the units of $d_k$. It is the median pairwise distance among unselected Earth land windows,

computed over all 3828 pairs of 88 windows on a regular grid inside the downloaded SRTM tiles, excluding any window within 10 km of a candidate centre. This gives $\tau_{\mathrm{slope}}$ = 5.8058° and $\tau_{\mathrm{rel}}$ = 77.1038 m at 60 m. The interpretation is a task-relevant contrast: a candidate that differs from the reference as much as a typical pair of real Earth landscapes differ from each other receives 0.5. The tolerance is a project definition, not an empirically validated threshold. It depends on the background sample: leaving one source tile out gives 4.52–6.34° and 55.1–88.6 m, and leaving one region out gives 3.68–9.42° and 42.7–146.7 m. The candidate windows were known before this rule was fixed, so it is not a blind test.
Feature selection and family score

Features whose window medians correlate at Spearman |ρ| ≥ 0.95 across the background windows are treated as one construct. Slope correlates with roughness (ρ = 0.998) and with local relief (ρ = 0.985), whereas relative elevation does not (ρ = -0.244 with slope). Slope and relative elevation are therefore the scored features; local relief and roughness are reported as diagnostics with zero weight. Within the terrain family $g$,
with $a_{\mathrm{slope}|g} = a_{\mathrm{rel}|g} = 0.5$. A family is eligible ($I_g = 1$) only if every scored feature is eligible; a family is never scored from an incomplete feature set.
Resolution floor and eligibility
The resolution floor is the distance produced by the measurement itself, not by a terrain difference:

where $\delta_{\mathrm{place},k}$ is the largest W1 between the reference window and the same window moved 2 km north, south, east and west, and $\delta_{\mathrm{dem},k}$ is the largest W1 between SRTMGL1 and NASADEM or Copernicus GLO-30 for the same Earth window (15 measured pairs). For Jezero, $\delta_{\mathrm{slope}}$ = 1.1708° and $\delta_{\mathrm{rel}}$ = 22.1523 m. A scored feature is used only if $\tau_k \ge 3\,\delta_k$; otherwise its distance is reported without a similarity. The floor never changes $s_k$. It decides eligibility and interpretation: when every scored distance is at or below its floor, the candidate is reported as not resolved from the reference by these tests. The tests are a 2 km reference move and a change of Earth DEM product; they do not cover every source of error, so the wording is limited to them. The lunar window fails the condition (moving it 2 km changes relative elevation by about 195 m against a 77 m tolerance), so lunar comparisons show distances without an index.
Observed index, evidence coverage and ranking
Each task profile assigns planned weights $w_g$ ($\sum_g w_g = 1$) to evidence families. With $I_g$ the eligibility indicator,

latex: A_{\mathrm{obs}} = 100 \times \frac{\sum_{g} w_{g} I_{g} S_{g}}{\sum_{g} w_{g} I_{g}}

text: $A_{\mathrm{obs}}$ is undefined, never zero, when no family qualifies. $C$ is the share of the planned profile weight that is measured and comparable; it is not statistical confidence and not DEM pixel coverage. Only terrain is currently measured, so $C$ = 1 for the terrain-analogy profile and 0.30, 0.80 and 0.35 for the balanced-science, rover-mobility and Mars-base field-testing profiles. A profile is ranked only if it is declared rankable, every task-critical family is eligible for every candidate and all candidates share one eligibility key (reference AOI, method, weights, scored features, tolerances, grid, DEM product and mask). Today only terrain analogy is ranked; the other profiles are reported as partial evidence or not assessed. If any task-critical gate fails, the overall API/export index is null; family measurements remain visible. Ties are formed from scenario ranges: each candidate's index is recomputed with the Earth window moved 2 km in four directions, the reference moved 2 km in four directions, each alternative DEM, the 120 and 240 m grids, all tolerances × 0.75 and × 1.25, and feature weights 0.25/0.75; candidates whose ranges overlap, chained in order of nominal index, share a competition rank. These ranges are scenario sensitivities, not confidence intervals.

text: Worked example: Atacama Desert (south window) compared with Jezero

Earth window earth-atacama-south-aoi-v1 (centre 24.2722° S, 69.9005° W; SRTMGL1.003 tile S25W070, extracted file SHA-256 31ff152bdf6000f3…; UTM zone 19S (EPSG:32719); ESA WorldCover v200 2021: cells ≥ 50 % built-up excluded, 0.00 % of cells excluded) is compared with mars-jezero-aoi-v1 (CTX DEM SHA-256 ba7f706ea1b5d63a…) under the terrain-analogy profile, analogue-method-v1.0.

caption: Table 7. Worked example at 60 m. d, τ and δ in the feature units; s and contributions from full-precision values.

text: With the full-precision values, $S_g$ = 0.5 × 0.986185 + 0.5 × 0.971893 = 0.979039 and $A_{\mathrm{obs}}$ = 97.9039, reported by the API as 97.90; the service and an independent recomputation with the reference arithmetic agree exactly (difference below 10⁻⁹ index points). Recombining the four-decimal similarities shown in the interface (0.9862 and 0.9719) gives 97.905, which differs in the last decimal only because of display rounding. Evidence coverage is $C$ = 1.00 (terrain only). Both scored distances are below their floors, so the window is not resolved from Jezero by these tests. Across 17 scenarios the index ranges 93.12–98.65; the window shares rank 1 with 4 other windows. Local relief (11.96 m) and roughness (1.02 m) are reported as diagnostics only.
Discrimination checks

Against Jezero, the 88 background windows have a median index of 87.4; 49% score 90 or more and 1% score 99 or more. Slope alone and relative elevation alone give 47% and 49% at 90 or more. The previous Phase 5 tolerances would give 55%, half the current tolerances 19% and double 58%. Against the other Mars references, 42–49 % of background windows score 90 or more. Synthetic controls scored 2.1 (a 15° tilted plane), 38.2 (150 m ridges every 2 km), 21.2 (rough 1,500 m fractal relief) and 100.0 (an identical copy of Jezero); a gentle 300 m fractal surface scored 88.4 because its distributions resemble Jezero's even though its spatial arrangement does not. The background windows come from tiles first downloaded for candidate sites: arid and mountainous regions are over-represented, and windows inside one region are spatially correlated. 4 regions, not 88 independent samples. The order of the five highest-scoring candidates is unchanged when the tolerance is recomputed with each region left out.
Limitations and validation status

items: The equations, the reference values of Equation 7, the W1 implementation, eligibility gates and determinism are verified by automated tests against an independent reference implementation. The scientific claim that the index identifies useful analogues has not been validated against expert-labelled analogues, expert-chosen negative controls or field outcomes.
Tolerances, weights and the redundancy threshold are project definitions. They are not fitted to labelled data and they depend on the background sample.
At a 60 m grid the index separates low-relief from rugged terrain but does not order low-relief windows; about half of unselected Earth windows score 90 or more against each Mars reference.
Distributions ignore spatial arrangement; no morphology descriptor is scored.
Only terrain is measured. Geology, temperature (which fails a comparability audit), water and ice, surface processes, habitability, field access and mission safety are not assessed.

SRTM (2000), CTX stereo (2006 onward) and LOLA record present-day surfaces. CTX stereo noise inflates slopes on very smooth plains, and planetary DEM vertical references differ from Earth's (relative elevation removes the offset but not tilts).
Existing NASA and USGS work supports measuring terrain and using Earth analogues for specific questions; it does not endorse this index, its weights or its tolerances.

Results: measured terrain resemblance, Atacama south and Jezero

On the two scored terrain features at a 60 m grid, the Atacama south window differs from the Jezero window by 0.82° in slope distribution and 15.6 m in relative-elevation distribution, giving an experimental terrain evidence index of 97.9 (scenario range 93.1–98.7) with 100 % terrain-profile coverage. Both differences are within the resolution floor of these tests, and the window shares rank 1 with 4 other low-relief windows whose order the data cannot resolve. The score is not distinctive: 17% of 88 unselected Earth windows score at least as high, and 49% score 90 or more. The result shows that the two windows share low-relief terrain at this scale; it does not show that Atacama is the best overall Mars analogue, and it says nothing about geology, habitability or the safety of a base or landing site.
